title: Allegations of systemic racism in Timmins are still before the Human Rights Tribunal
subtitle: Case alleges discrimination by five service providers in deaths of Joey Knapaysweet and Agnes Sutherland
article: The Human Rights Tribunal application alleging discrimination by public service providers in Timmins is advancing, more than six years after the deaths of the two people at the centre of it.
21-year-old Joey Knapaysweet and 62-year-old Agnes Sutherland left the remote community of Fort Albany, near Ontario's James Bay coast, to seek medical care in Timmins.
Knapaysweet was shot by Timmins police after fleeing the hospital emergency room on February 3, 2018.
Sutherland died the next day in hospital after being arrested and jailed following a disturbance at a Timmins shelter.
The deaths sparked outrage, with prominent First Nation leaders asking if systemic racism was a contributing factor.

Ontario's Special Investigations Unit later cleared Timmins police of wrongdoing in those two separate incidents, saying Sutherland had died of natural causes associated with her diabetes and heart disease, and that force had been justified in Knapaysweet's case.

After the deaths, Ontario Human Rights Commissioner Renu Mandhane went on a fact-finding mission in the region, and concluded that racism against Indigenous people in Timmins appeared to be both pervasive and normalized.
The Ontario Human Rights Commission joined the families of Sutherland and Knapaysweet in their application with Ontario's Human Rights Tribunal in 2020.

The application alleges discrimination by five of the city's social service providers: Timmins and District Hospital, Timmins Police Services Board, a women's shelter now known as Ellevive, Cochrane District Detox Centre, and the Cochrane District Social Services Administration Board.
CBC news obtained a copy of a procedural decision made by the Tribunal earlier in September.
The document shows that the social service providers and the Sutherland and Knapaysweet families did not agree to mediation.
It also indicated that the Tribunal will hear the files separately, as there are "distinct issues at hand" with "little overlap in the witnesses and evidence to be heard."
The decision reveals the Tribunal denied a request for a summary hearing - meaning one of the social service providers sought to have the application dismissed, and the Tribunal disagreed.
This means they determined that the allegations could amount to discrimination under the Ontario Human Rights Code.
Shannon Sproule is a lawyer and investigator at Turnpenney Milne LLP. She says it is unusual for the Ontario Human Rights Commission to intervene in applications before the Tribunal.
"It has to be fairly significant and you'll typically see it for systemic issues [such as] race based discrimination where they are of the view that a remedy of grander scale is warranted," she said.

Sproule says there's been a general backlog facing the Tribunal, and that this, combined with the Commission being an intervener and the fact that the families are advancing the application on behalf of Knapaysweet and Sutherland could explain the long delays in the case.
Sproule also says the Tribunal's discussion of the deaths will have a different scope than the investigation that was carried out by Ontario's Special Investigations Unit.
"They may have determined there was no wrongdoing, but that may not capture the full realm of the Human Rights Code and what's possible when examining systemic discrimination," she said.
"This case could set a precedent."
